extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists and non-specialists wanting to assess scientific claims
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for non-specialists to judge the quality and reliability of evidence cited in articles, adverts, policy proposals or social media. Covers how to spot study types, common pitfalls, statistical issues, survey problems and conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is it based on scientific research?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether claims are actually based on published scientific research rather than authoritative-sounding text or marketing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A full reference to a scientific paper should be provided (authors, title, journal, year, pages). If an article doesn’t reference scientific research, that’s not a good start. Websites selling products may present 'science-y' information to imply credibility; always ask: are claims based on published scientific research, or not?

rubrics_metrics.name: Is it peer reviewed?
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask whether the research has been assessed by other experts (peer review) before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review means other scientific experts checked the paper for validity, significance and originality. Not all journals are peer reviewed — check the journal website. Some findings reported in headlines are not peer reviewed (conference talks, single opinions). Post-publication peer review (blogs, expert commentary) can indicate how a study was received by the community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animal studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence coming from animal experiments rather than human subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Animal studies are useful models but are never a direct substitute for human tests; differences between animals and humans can be subtle or substantial. Treat claims based only on animal research with caution — they don’t prove safety or effectiveness in humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: In vitro (test tube) studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies of cells, tissues or microbes outside a living organism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In vitro experiments (e.g., cells in a petri dish) help understand mechanisms but are hard to reproduce the 'real world' conditions of a whole organism. Many sensational claims (new cures or hazards) are based only on in vitro work; check relevance to real-world exposure and biology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studies observing people (epidemiological/observational)
rubrics_metrics.description: Population studies that report associations between exposures and outcomes in real-life conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational studies can flag associations but cannot establish causation because of uncontrolled confounders (lifestyle, diet, healthcare access). Large sample sizes help but causal links generally require follow-up with more controlled studies (e.g., RCTs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Randomised controlled trials (RCTs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Controlled experiments where participants are randomly assigned to intervention or control groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RCTs are the 'gold standard' because they attempt to eliminate confounding. Well-conducted RCTs provide a strong basis for claims about effectiveness. Note: RCTs are not always possible, practical or ethical in every area (e.g., some policy or education questions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical trials and trial phases
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence from clinical trials, typically in sequential phases assessing safety and effectiveness of medical treatments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phase 1: small initial safety studies (not designed for effectiveness); Phase 2: safety and preliminary effectiveness in a small group (promising but not definitive); Phase 3: large trials (hundreds/thousands) to measure effectiveness — only after Phase 3 can licensing applications be made. 'In clinical trials' does not imply imminent availability or proven safety/effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies that pool and analyse all relevant available data to assess the strength of evidence across multiple studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviews follow quality-control guidelines to exclude poor studies and are generally better at assessing evidence than single studies. Meta-analysis is a statistical pooling method. Beware: not every 'review' is a systematic review — editorial reviews may cherry-pick studies. A systematic review of weak underlying studies remains weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance of the study
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the study actually tests what the claim asserts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t assume a paper supports a claim — check 'what’s actually being tested'. A reputable paper can still be irrelevant to the specific claim being made. Always ask whether the subjects, interventions, outcomes and settings match the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wider body of evidence and replication
rubrics_metrics.description: How the study's results fit with other research in the same area and whether findings have been replicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single study rarely overturns an established body of evidence; if a study’s conclusions contradict the majority of research, that’s a warning sign. Look for subsequent studies, systematic reviews, or expert commentary to see if findings have been replicated or challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study size (sample size)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the study included enough participants or observations to support its conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small studies are more likely to produce chance results; dramatic headlines are often based on small samples. There is no single 'magic' sample size, but context matters (e.g., political polls often use ~1,000 respondents). Compare small-study findings against larger studies in the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dose and exposure relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the amount or dose used in the study reflects real-world exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects depend on dose: laboratory or animal studies might use much higher doses than humans encounter. Ask: what was the dose and how does it compare to likely real-world exposure? A chemical is not simply 'dangerous' or 'safe' — it depends on amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance versus practical importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish statistical significance (unlikely due to chance) from practical or real-world significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statistically significant result may be mathematically non-random but still trivially small in real terms. Don’t be fooled by the term 'statistically significant' — ask if the effect size matters in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression to the mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The tendency for extreme results to move closer to average on subsequent measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extremely large or dramatic findings in one study may be followed by more typical results later; a big initial effect is often reduced in later studies. Treat single extreme findings with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outliers
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme values that may be presented to make results seem more dramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists or promoters may use the most extreme number from a range (phrases like 'up to' or 'as much as') which can mislead. Check whether reported values are typical or exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative risk versus absolute risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether risk is reported as a relative percentage change or as the absolute chance of an outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting a percentage increase without the underlying absolute risk can exaggerate importance. To judge whether a change matters you need to know the initial (absolute) risk as well as the relative change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anecdotes, testimonials and personal stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of individual stories or case studies to illustrate or support claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdotes are not representative and often lack factual backing. Personal stories do not substitute for scientific research; ask if there is any scientific evidence to support the anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys — who commissioned the survey?
rubrics_metrics.description: Who paid for or commissioned the survey and whether they may have a vested interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial or PR-motivated surveys may be designed to create a news hook or favourable coverage. Knowing the commissioner helps assess potential bias or spin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys — who was interviewed (representativeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the people surveyed properly represent the wider population claimed to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-representative samples (e.g., interviewing commuters at 7am to represent all Londoners) can skew results. Check whether the sampling method matches the population the survey claims to describe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys — how many people were asked and response rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The number asked and the proportion who responded, which affect reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey headlines often omit how many were asked or what fraction responded; low response rates or small samples can make results meaningless. No universal 'magic' number exists, but context-specific benchmarks (e.g., ~1,000 for many national polls) are useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveys — how were the questions asked (question design and administration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether question wording, order or the person asking influenced responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leading questions or interviewer effects can bias answers; respondents may be embarrassed, forgetful, or answer in socially desirable ways. Question wording and method matter a lot for survey validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who funded the study (interests and conflicts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of funding sources and potential vested interests that may influence research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the money: funders can bias research design, reporting or emphasis. Academics should disclose interests in journals. However, funding alone is not a definitive guide — good research can come from vested organisations and biased conclusions can come from neutral parties.
